testerProfile.focus: the spike and its "Ouch!" message are allowed on purpose

comparablesNote: Comparable games from the Tester profile: PBS KIDS mazes, Pac-Man, Monument Valley.

summary: Mazle's biggest gap for 5-7 year olds is that it communicates everything through text and silence: no voice, no sound effects, and a debug overlay left on screen, where PBS KIDS mazes and Monument Valley lean on voice-over or wordless visual cues so pre-readers never have to read. The soft-fail spike and instant reset are already well-tuned for this age group and shouldn't change. Closing the audio, celebration, and stray-debug-info gaps would bring mazle much closer to genre norms for the youngest bracket without touching the core maze mechanic.

items.they_do: PBS KIDS has a character speak the goal aloud with a replay-voice button; Monument Valley is fully wordless, using glowing handles to show what to do.
items.we_do: Level 1 opens straight into the maze with a 4-line, ~30-word text-only controls box (WASD/arrows, mouse look, touch drag zones) and no spoken or visual goal cue.
items.suggestion: Add a 3-word spoken line ('Find the door!') via the Web Speech API when Level 1 starts, and make the exit door glow or pulse so the goal is visible without reading.

items.they_do: PBS KIDS runs full voice-over and music throughout; Monument Valley has ambient music and musical feedback on every drag, with no voice-over.
items.we_do: The build ships 0 audio assets total, with no speechSynthesis, WebAudio, or <audio> elements anywhere.
items.suggestion: Add a short looping ambient track (three.js/Web Audio) plus a one-shot footstep or 'whoosh' sound tied to movement so the game isn't silent for a pre-reader.

items.they_do: Both keep the screen free of anything but game content and controls sized for the player; Monument Valley shows no fail state or stray UI at all.
items.we_do: A dev-only 'FPS: Infinity / Position' debug overlay is visible on every screenshot, and no pause, mute, or quit/home control exists anywhere (fails rubric R16).
items.suggestion: Hide the FPS/position readout behind a dev-only flag (e.g. ?debug=1) and add a single home-icon button in a corner that returns to Level 1.

items.they_do: Instructions are audio-first with large touch targets, so nothing depends on reading.
items.we_do: The controls box and the 8-word spike message ('Ouch! A spike sent you back to the start.') both exceed the ~5-words-per-instruction target for this bracket, with no audio pairing.
items.suggestion: Shorten the spike message to 'Ouch! Back to start.' (4 words) and play a short 'ouch' sound effect alongside it, keeping the spike itself unchanged since it's allowed on purpose.

items.they_do: Pac-Man gives tight, instant response with a distinct sound on every dot eaten, so feedback is constant.
items.we_do: There is no sound-on-input anywhere, including no audio cue when the player reaches the door and wins.
items.suggestion: Add a short chime (WebAudio, 1-2 notes) that plays the instant the player touches the door, before the 'You found the way out!' text appears.

items.they_do: Pac-Man awards fruit bonuses along the way; PBS KIDS games sometimes award stickers or collectibles on success.
items.we_do: Winning only shows the text 'You found the way out!' with a 'Play again' button — no stars, collectibles, or unlocks appear anywhere in the evidence.
items.suggestion: Show one earned star (not a 1-3 rating tied to speed or perfection, just a single star for finishing) on the win screen to give a small visible reward.

items.they_do: Monument Valley clearly highlights interactive parts of the world so the player always knows what to do next.
items.we_do: The maze corridors give no visual cue toward the door — the player must explore blind, relying only on the text controls box read at the start.
items.suggestion: Add a faint directional glow or floor arrow near the player that points toward the door, especially useful for the youngest 5-year-olds in the bracket.

items.they_do: PBS KIDS mazes are very gentle with almost no way to fail outright; Pac-Man ramps difficulty gradually level to level.
items.we_do: Only Level 1 has been measured, with no data yet on how maze size or spike placement changes across levels.
items.suggestion: Keep the first 1-2 levels short and nearly impossible to fail (few corridors, spike far from the direct path), and add a small 'Level 1' counter on screen so progress is visible.

present.evidence: Touching the spike is an instant, no-cost soft fail that resets the player to the exact start position (2.5, 0.0, 2.5) rather than showing a game-over screen or menu.
Winning shows 'You found the way out!' with a 'Play again' button; no autoplay into a next level is implied by the evidence.
Hitting the spike costs only a reset to the start position, with no life system, item loss, or level restart.

missing.suggestion: Add a small friendly character or arrow that appears at level start and points toward the door, since pre-readers respond better to a character than to a text controls box.
Replace or supplement the 4-line text controls box with an animated hand/arrow showing a drag-to-move gesture on the first few seconds of Level 1.
Add a small sound effect to the 'Play again' button press and to movement start, since the build currently has zero audio assets.
Pair the win text with a brief visual flourish (confetti or a color flash) and a short sound within ~0.5s of reaching the door.
Add a single star reward on the win screen for finishing the level, without requiring perfection to earn it.
If the player idles or loops in the maze for ~15-20 seconds, show a gentle glow toward the door, sooner than for older brackets.
Add a simple level indicator (e.g. 'Level 1') so the child can see progress once more levels exist.
Once stars or collectibles exist, let a few earned by playing unlock a cosmetic (e.g. wall or floor color), never sold or bought.

ourProfile.source: bot-run (key screenshots only; no play.json yet)

profile.onboarding: No menu — Level 1 opens straight into the 3D maze with a controls box in the corner (4 lines, ~30 words: WASD/arrows, mouse look, touch drag zones); not measured in taps-to-play since no bot play.json exists, but zero taps are needed to start moving.
profile.controls: Keyboard W/↑ forward, S/↓ back, A/← and D/→ strafe, mouse to look; touch equivalent is drag left side to move, drag right side to look.
profile.core_loop: Walk the maze corridors, avoid the spike trap, find and reach the exit door.
profile.goals_and_rewards: One goal per level (reach the door); winning shows the text "You found the way out!" with a "Play again" button — no stars, collectibles, or unlocks seen in the evidence.
profile.difficulty_curve: Not measured beyond Level 1; touching the spike is an instant, no-cost soft fail (message + reset to the exact start position 2.5, 0.0, 2.5) rather than a life system or game-over screen.
profile.game_feel: Not measured — the only performance data is the decorative "FPS: Infinity" debug readout, and there is no sound-on-input since the build ships 0 audio assets.
profile.art_and_audio: Flat-shaded, low-poly geometric style (grey walls, green floor, pale-blue sky/ceiling panel, brown door); no audio at all — 0 audio files, no speechSynthesis, no WebAudio, no <audio> elements.
profile.session_length: Not measured (no play.json/time-to-win data); position readouts show the player traveled from (2.5, 2.5) to the door at roughly (27, 22) over the run.
profile.usability: Fails rubric R16: no pause, mute, or quit/home control appears on any screen — the only interactive element anywhere is "Play again" after winning. A dev-only "FPS/Position" debug overlay is visible on every screenshot and should be hidden before shipping.
profile.accessibility: Contrast is strong (white/light text on solid dark panels in every screenshot, comfortably above 4.5:1) and no cues rely on color alone. However all instructions are text-only with no audio pairing, and the controls block plus the 8-word death message ("Ouch! A spike sent you back to the start.") exceed the ~5-words-per-instruction target for this bracket.
profile.notes: failing-spike.png and failing-spike-later.png (~1s apart) show an identical frame, so how long the failure message lingers or whether it blocks movement isn't confirmed from evidence; the spike hazard itself is a mild, cartoonish grey cone trap with an "Ouch!" response, not a scary character.
